title: Israeli categories
hookLine: most Israelis describe themselves as secular, traditional, religious or Haredi

cards: Ask an Israeli about religion, and the answer may not be the name of a movement at all. Often it is one of four Hebrew words. A taxi driver says one.
The woman in the next seat on the bus says another. A soldier home for the weekend says a third, and the young man in the black coat at the corner says the fourth. Four words.
They describe how a person lives. They are today's word.

teach.b: Israeli categories. One word at a time. First, hiloni: secular.
Some readers hear in it chol, the ordinary, the weekday, the opposite of holy. The Torah tells the priests to "put difference between holy and unholy," and in Hebrew that unholy is chol.
As Shabbat ends, the Havdalah blessing praises God who separates holy from ordinary.
A hiloni Israeli lives mostly on the ordinary side of that line, in Hebrew, with the Bible as the people's story, and may still light candles at Hanukkah or sit at a seder.

teach.h: MASORTI: SOME OF WHAT'S HANDED DOWN.
teach.b: Second, masorti: traditional, keeping what is handed down. A masorti Israeli keeps some of it, often Friday night and the festivals, without keeping all of it.
Careful: Masorti is also the name of the Conservative movement in Israel, but as a word about yourself it simply means traditional. Tomorrow stays with this middle. Third, dati: religious.
Some readers hear in it dat, the word the book of Esther uses for the king's law.
A dati Israeli keeps halakha; some call themselves dati leumi, national religious, the Religious Zionists from earlier in this block.
Fourth, haredi, the Haredi communities from earlier in the block; the name echoes Isaiah's words to those who tremble: "ye that tremble at his word."
Here is the turn: these are words people choose for themselves, and they overlap.
Someone can be hiloni and fast on Yom Kippur. Someone masorti can pray every morning. The lines are blurry because they describe lives, not membership cards.

how: Israeli Jews may describe themselves as hiloni (secular), masorti (traditional), dati (religious) or haredi, and these self-chosen words shape everyday conversation about schools, neighborhoods and Shabbat.

games.q: an Israeli lights candles and makes kiddush on Friday night, keeps the festivals, and spends Shabbat afternoon at the beach. which word might they choose?
games.why: masorti, traditional: keeping some of what's handed down without keeping all of it. but people choose these words for themselves, and the lines blur.

practice: On each out-breath, say one word quietly: hiloni, and let the ordinary weekday come to mind; masorti, and something handed down to you; dati, someone who keeps a whole law with care; haredi, those who tremble at God's word.
Go round again, slower, until the four words feel like four neighbors rather than four boxes. If you pray, you can hold all four in your prayer.
